newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tung names reformist lawyer as HK Chief Justice.
newsitem.headline: Tung names reformist lawyer as HK Chief Justice.

text.p: A reform-minded lawyer was named Hong Kong's chief judge on Tuesday to occupy a potentially politico-legal "hot seat" under Chinese rule.
Fellow barristers, democracy campaigners and Governor Chris Patten applauded the choice of 48-year-old Andrew Li, announced by future leader Tung Chee-hwa, Beijing's anointed chief executive.
The appointment of the Hong Kong-born, Cambridge-educated Chinese lawyer came amid concern in the West and here about Tung's plans to curb civil liberties.
Members of the legal profession hailed the decision, some relieved that a respected fellow-professional lawyer is to be the territory's top judge after China takes over in just 42 days.
Li will head the Court of Final Appeal, the last recourse of justice for Hong Kong's 6.4 million, mainly-Chinese residents after Britain's withdrawal.

Patten, who frequently clashes on policy with his designated successor Tung, said: "This is excellent news and will be greeted with real enthusiasm by the legal profession, the community and by all those who know him in other countries."
"With Andrew Li you can't be getting a puppet," Margaret Ng, who represents legal interests in the Legislative Council, told Reuters.
"That the government starts with someone who is not a puppet is very encouraging," she said.
She hoped that Li would be able to maintain the independence of the judiciary as he was steeped in a Common Law tradition, shaped by British courts over the centuries.
"He is a very rational person, he has a great deal of self control, he is very careful, he habitually collects views...he is a prudent individual," Ng said.
She said that Li also had a reformist streak which made a good combination for a Chief Justice.
Leader of the democratic party Martin Lee said Li commanded the respect of the bar and was a man of integrity, but that his appointment had to be vetted by a body of dubious legal status.

"This appointment of the chief justice, as well as the appointment of all others have to be approved by the (China-nominated successor) legislature, only a provisional legislature--the constitutional status of which remains in doubt," Lee told Reuters.
If a legal challenge to the provisional legislature's legitimacy reached the Court of Final Appeal, it could create a constitutional crisis, Lee said.
"How can these judges act when their own appointment is called into question?" Lee said.
The Judicial Officers Recommendation Commission, a panel set up by Tung in April and which itself will assume office on July 1, recommended Li for the post, Tung said in a statement.
"I am pleased to accept the JORC (designate)'s recommendation on his appointment as Chief Justice of the Court of Final Appeal," Tung said.
The future Secretary of Justice Elsie Leung will move a resolution on May 24 to seek support from the provisional legislature for Li's appointment, Tung said.
China plans to replace the current elected legislative council with the provisional chamber, formed under Beijing's auspices in December, on July 1.
A Court of Final Appeal in Hong Kong, headed by the chief justice, will replace London's Privy Council as the place of last resort following Hong Kong's return to China.
Cheng Yuen, 83, and a former golf caddie fighting for a pension, is to be the last Hong Kong litigant at the Commonwealth's highest court on June 19 in London.
